<article>
Lindell withholds $825,000 recount payment, calls Minnesota plan 'unlawful'

MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — Mike Lindell's campaign on Monday withheld the $825,000 payment required to trigger a statewide hand recount of the Republican primary for Minnesota governor, calling the state's proposed recount scope "unlawful."

The MyPillow founder, who secured the endorsement of President Donald Trump for the race, finished second to Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth in the August 11 primary, receiving 134,282 votes to Demuth's 179,683. On election night, Lindell said he would not concede until every vote was counted and that his team had spotted "anomalies" it needed time to review.

Lindell's team argues that the Secretary of State's plan would count only the votes cast for Lindell and Demuth, leaving out the votes for the other five Republican candidates on the ballot. The campaign cited Minnesota Statute 204C.35, which it says defines a recount as determining "the number of votes validly cast for the office or question to be recounted."

Lindell has asked the state to waive the payment deadline until a court can rule on the scope of the recount.

"Our office provided the contingent recount plan to Mr. Lindell after it was approved by the State Canvassing Board on Aug. 18," a spokesperson for Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon said. "The plan follows state law and administrative rules on recount procedures, and is consistent with plans of its kind for the past two decades."

The contingency plan, released last week, names Paul Linnell, the office's director of elections, as state recount official, with authority to appoint deputy officials at counting sites across the state. The recount would be open to the public and media.

There have been no official findings of fraud or irregularity in the primary results. Lindell, who described his recount effort as a "gateway to getting rid of" electronic voting machines, had gathered with supporters at the Hilton Hotel in downtown Minneapolis on election day.

Demuth will face Sen. Amy Klobuchar in the November 3 general election. Governor Tim Walz, who is not running again, presides over a state where the recount dispute has become its own campaign story.
</article>

At least 7 dead after days of historic flooding in Indiana

INDIANAPOLIS (AP) — Days of storms and record-setting flooding in Indiana left at least seven people dead as floodwaters receded Sunday and the state began recovery.

A 4-year-old boy, three men and three women were among those who had died since the storms began Aug. 11, said Liz Woods, a spokesperson for the state Department of Homeland Security.

Among the latest confirmed victims was James Briar, a 31-year-old cyclist found dead early Sunday in a hole that opened up on a washed-out road in Henry County, east of Indianapolis. Henry County Coroner Brian Clark said Briar appears to have gone around a barricade and fallen into the collapsed road in New Castle. His body was discovered just before 4 a.m. Aug. 16 and he was pronounced dead at the scene.

Other victims included Matthew Morey, 19, of Delaware County, who drowned in the Mississinewa River, and a 58-year-old woman in Delaware County whose home was struck when a tree came through her bedroom window during the storm.

President Donald Trump approved an emergency declaration for Indiana on Saturday, which allows the Federal Emergency Management Agency to provide resources to the state after severe storms, straight-line winds, tornadoes and flooding that swept over half of the state's 92 counties.

Heavy rain pushed the White River to a crest of approximately 24.60 feet in Hamilton County around 3:30 a.m. Aug. 15, breaking a record set more than 100 years ago, county officials said.

At the peak of the flooding, more than 350,000 residents lost power, including almost all of Lake County, and the Indiana National Guard was deployed to assist local responders.
</article>

A 4-year-old boy, three men and three women were among those who had died since the storms began Aug. 11, said Liz Woods, a spokesperson for the state Department of Homeland Security.

Among the latest confirmed victims was James Briar, a 31-year-old cyclist found dead early Sunday in a hole that opened up on a washed-out road in Henry County, east of Indianapolis. Henry County Coroner Brian Clark said Briar appears to have gone around a barricade and fallen into the collapsed road in New Castle. His body was discovered just before 4 a.m. Aug. 16 and he was pronounced dead at the scene.

Other victims included Matthew Morey, 19, of Delaware County, who drowned in the Mississinewa River, and a 58-year-old woman in Delaware County whose home was struck when a tree came through her bedroom window during the storm.

President Donald Trump approved an emergency declaration for Indiana on Saturday, which allows the Federal Emergency Management Agency to provide resources to the state after severe storms, straight-line winds, tornadoes and flooding that swept over half of the state's 92 counties.

Heavy rain pushed the White River to a crest of approximately 24.60 feet in Hamilton County around 3:30 a.m. Aug. 15, breaking a record set more than 100 years ago, county officials said.

At the peak of the flooding, more than 350,000 residents lost power, including almost all of Lake County, and the Indiana National Guard was deployed to assist local responders.
</article>

<article>
Somali Airlines to resume flights after 35-year hiatus

MOGADISHU — Somalia's national carrier, Somali Airlines, is expected to resume flights in September 2026, more than three decades after it stopped operating following the collapse of the country's central government in 1991.

Ahmed Moalin, director of the Somali Civil Aviation Authority, said Saturday that preparations to relaunch the carrier had been completed and that flights were expected to begin next month.

"Somali Airlines is in the final stage," Moalin said. "I think the first flight will begin in September."

Somali Airlines, established in 1964 and once known as the "White Star," was the country's flag carrier, operating domestic and international routes, before its operations were halted by the civil war that followed the ouster of President Siad Barre in 1991.

The planned revival follows several earlier missed restart targets. The government announced an agreement involving two Airbus A320 aircraft in July 2025 as the first step toward reviving the carrier, and in October 2025 the transport ministry said the airline would begin services by the end of that year. That did not happen.

Mogadishu's Aden Adde International Airport is currently served by international carriers including Ethiopian Airlines, Qatar Airways and Turkish Airlines, and for more than 30 years air travel in Somalia has largely been handled by private and foreign airlines.

Officials say the return of the national carrier is meant to improve domestic and regional connectivity, strengthen links with the Somali diaspora, create jobs and support trade.
</article>

Ahmed Moalin, director of the Somali Civil Aviation Authority, said Saturday that preparations to relaunch the carrier had been completed and that flights were expected to begin next month.

"Somali Airlines is in the final stage," Moalin said. "I think the first flight will begin in September."

Somali Airlines, established in 1964 and once known as the "White Star," was the country's flag carrier, operating domestic and international routes, before its operations were halted by the civil war that followed the ouster of President Siad Barre in 1991.

The planned revival follows several earlier missed restart targets. The government announced an agreement involving two Airbus A320 aircraft in July 2025 as the first step toward reviving the carrier, and in October 2025 the transport ministry said the airline would begin services by the end of that year. That did not happen.

Mogadishu's Aden Adde International Airport is currently served by international carriers including Ethiopian Airlines, Qatar Airways and Turkish Airlines, and for more than 30 years air travel in Somalia has largely been handled by private and foreign airlines.

Officials say the return of the national carrier is meant to improve domestic and regional connectivity, strengthen links with the Somali diaspora, create jobs and support trade.
</article>

Somali Airlines to resume flights after 35-year hiatus

MOGADISHU — Somalia's national carrier, Somali Airlines, is expected to resume flights in September 2026, more than three decades after it stopped operating following the collapse of the country's central government in 1991.

Ahmed Moalin, director of the Somali Civil Aviation Authority, said Saturday that preparations to relaunch the carrier had been completed and that flights were expected to begin next month.

"Somali Airlines is in the final stage," Moalin said. "I think the first flight will begin in September."

Somali Airlines, established in 1964 and once known as the "White Star," was the country's flag carrier, operating domestic and international routes, before its operations were halted by the civil war that followed the ouster of President Siad Barre in 1991.

The planned revival follows several earlier missed restart targets. The government announced an agreement involving two Airbus A320 aircraft in July 2025 as the first step toward reviving the carrier, and in October 2025 the transport ministry said the airline would begin services by the end of that year. That did not happen.

Mogadishu's Aden Adde International Airport is currently served by international carriers including Ethiopian Airlines, Qatar Airways and Turkish Airlines, and for more than 30 years air travel in Somalia has largely been handled by private and foreign airlines.

Officials say the return of the national carrier is meant to improve domestic and regional connectivity, strengthen links with the Somali diaspora, create jobs and support trade.

The regulator also pointed to a product change in early March, when Discord introduced end-to-end encryption to its communications, making the company's access to in-stream content even more limited.

Discord faces fines of up to 50 million reais (about $9.67 million) per violation.

<article>
TikTok pays $400 million in US children's privacy settlement

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — TikTok and its Chinese parent company ByteDance on Friday agreed to a $400 million settlement to resolve the US Justice Department's lawsuit alleging the short-video app violated children's online privacy.

Under the settlement, TikTok will pay $300 million immediately and an additional $100 million upon entry of an order vacating a prior consent decree entered in 2019 with the Federal Trade Commission against TikTok's predecessor, Musical.ly.

The settlement represents one of the largest recoveries ever obtained in a case under the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, a federal law enacted in 2000 that requires services directed at children to obtain parental consent before collecting personal information from users under age 13.

The Justice Department filed the lawsuit in 2024 in the US District Court for the Central District of California, on referral from the Federal Trade Commission. The suit accused TikTok and ByteDance of collecting vast amounts of data on millions of users under 13, failing to honor requests from parents who wanted their children's accounts deleted, and not deleting accounts even when the companies knew they belonged to children under 13.

As part of the 2019 consent decree, Musical.ly had paid a $5.7 million fine for COPPA violations.

The justice department said that since it sued the platform, TikTok has "undergone significant changes," including to its ownership, privacy practices and platform controls for young users. The settlement involves TikTok's operations in China.

COPPA is also the law that dozens of US states are now suing Meta over.
</article>

KUALA LUMPUR (Reuters) — Malaysia's Johor Darul Ta'zim (JDT) set a new world record on Friday, extending their unbeaten run in top-flight league football to 109 matches after a 3-0 victory over Kuching City in the opening match of the 2026/27 Malaysian Super League season.

Marcos Guilherme scored in the 11th minute, and Oscar Arribas and Shahab Zahedi found the net in the second half as the 12-time defending champions won in front of a packed crowd at Sultan Ibrahim Stadium.

The win took JDT one game clear of the previous mark of 108 top-flight league games without defeat, set by Ivory Coast's ASEC Mimosas between 1989 and 1994. JDT had matched that record in May with a 14-1 demolition of Kelantan The Real Warriors, the biggest winning margin in the league's history, in the final match of last season.

The Southern Tigers have not lost a league match since a 1-0 defeat by Terengganu in April 2021, and have gone unbeaten through the last four Super League campaigns. In the run's only serious scare, they came from 2-1 down against Sri Pahang in May 2022 before all-time record scorer Bergson levelled in the 88th minute.

The club is owned by Johor Crown Prince Tunku Ismail, whose arrival more than a decade ago set the team on its path of dominance, and is managed by the Spanish coach Xisco Munoz.

JDT were also drawn 3-3 against Chelsea in a preseason friendly this summer, and remain the only Southeast Asian club to have won the AFC Cup, in 2015.

NAIROBI (AFP) — All seven people on board a safari helicopter, six passengers and a pilot, were killed on Wednesday when the aircraft crashed in the foothills of Mount Ololokwe in Samburu County, central Kenya, authorities said.

Kenya's Civil Aviation Authority said the group's Eurocopter EC130 B4, operated by Lady Lori Helicopters, crashed at 9:13 a.m. (06:13 GMT) after departing the Loisaba Conservancy on a scenic charter toward the Ewaso Ng'iro area. The Kenya Red Cross said difficult terrain and a fire at the crash site hampered search and recovery efforts.

Among the dead were Michele Sensi-Contugi, 44, director general of Ecuador's strategic intelligence center, and his wife, Stephany Hollihan, 42, a fashion designer who also held US citizenship.

A US State Department spokesperson said five of the six passengers killed were US citizens, and NBC News reported that one of them was Jose Suarez, a prominent television executive. The other American victims were from South Florida.

Sensi-Contugi, a former businessman and close associate of Ecuador's right-wing President Daniel Noboa, was appointed head of national intelligence in January 2024. Noboa declared three days of national mourning and ordered a state funeral.

The pilot was identified as Josh Outram, an American.

Mount Ololokwe is a sacred mountain for the Samburu people, its summit rising 2,000 metres above sea level, and it is a popular hiking destination where companies offer helicopter flyovers.

DAMASCUS (Reuters) — The United States on Monday removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, lifting what Damascus says was the last major barrier to private-sector investment in the country as Washington deepens ties to the new Syrian government.

The removal, posted on the U.S. Treasury's website, took effect after a 45-day congressional review period triggered when President Donald Trump formally notified Congress on July 8 of his intention to rescind the decades-old designation. Syria had been on the list since 1979, when Washington accused the government of former President Hafez al-Assad of supporting armed groups, and it remained throughout the rule of his son, Bashar al-Assad, who was toppled by rebels led by current President Ahmed al-Sharaa in December 2024.

" These actions were all taken in recognition of the positive actions taken and further commitments by the Syrian government under President Ahmed al-Sharaa to fully distance Syria from acts of international terrorism," U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement.

Monday's announcement also revoked the designation of al-Nusrah Front, the group formerly led by al-Sharaa and known as Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), as a global terrorist organization. HTS was once al-Qaeda's official branch in Syria. The move leaves Cuba, North Korea and Iran as the three countries designated by Washington as state sponsors of terrorism.

Trump notified Congress after meeting al-Sharaa in Ankara in July, telling the Syrian president in a letter that he had promised to remove all barriers preventing Syria from rebuilding.

Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani said there is "no longer any obstacle to investment, doing business and rebuilding economic life in Syria," and the country's central bank chief, Safwat Raslan, said the government is building a modern financial system.

US envoy Tom Barrack called the end of the designation a decisive step in Syria's journey "from isolation to partnership."

France's top court blocks social media ban for under-15s

PARIS (Reuters) — France's top court on Friday blocked a bill banning social media access for under-15s, saying it infringed upon freedom of expression and delivering a setback for President Emmanuel Macron, who asked his government to rewrite the legislation.

The Constitutional Council, ruling on two parliamentary referrals, found that Article 1 of the law "constitutes an infringement that is neither appropriate, necessary, nor proportionate" to the freedom of expression and communication of children under 15.

The law would have barred children younger than 15 from opening a social media account from September 1, and platforms would have had to close existing accounts within four months using age verification approved by the French privacy regulator. French lawmakers approved the ban in July, which would have made France the first European country to enact such a measure, after Australia barred under-16s from platforms including Facebook, TikTok and YouTube in December.

The council said that by prohibiting minors under 15 from accessing certain online services, the law inherently requires every person, even an adult, to prove their age before accessing them, and the legislature did not establish the conditions and limits of that proof. It also said the ban's scope was too broad, reaching collaboration tools, communication apps and social games whose risks for minors are not established.

The Elysee said Macron ordered Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to re-work the bill to take the Constitutional Council's concerns into account. Macron is determined the reform take effect before Spring 2027, when France holds a presidential election in which he cannot run for a third term.

PARIS (Reuters) — France's top court on Friday blocked a bill banning social media access for under-15s, saying it infringed upon freedom of expression and delivering a setback for President Emmanuel Macron, who asked his government to rewrite the legislation.

The Constitutional Council, ruling on two parliamentary referrals, found that Article 1 of the law "constitutes an infringement that is neither appropriate, necessary, nor proportionate" to the freedom of expression and communication of children under 15.

The law would have barred children younger than 15 from opening a social media account from September 1, and platforms would have had to close existing accounts within four months using age verification approved by the French privacy regulator. French lawmakers approved the ban in July, which would have made France the first European country to enact such a measure, after Australia barred under-16s from platforms including Facebook, TikTok and YouTube in December.

The council said that by prohibiting minors under 15 from accessing certain online services, the law inherently requires every person, even an adult, to prove their age before accessing them, and the legislature did not establish the conditions and limits of that proof. It also said the ban's scope was too broad, reaching collaboration tools, communication apps and social games whose risks for minors are not established.

The Elysee said Macron ordered Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to re-work the bill to take the Constitutional Council's concerns into account. Macron is determined the reform take effect before Spring 2027, when France holds a presidential election in which he cannot run for a third term.

Lala Batters Hawaii
NASA Earth Observatory | August 18, 2026. Story by Lindsey Doermann. Images by Lauren Dauphin.

The powerful storm delivered extreme rainfall and damaging winds to the state, passing the Island of Hawaiʻi as a category 1 hurricane.

The spiraling clouds of a tropical storm are centered near the Hawaiian island of Kauaʻi. [August 16, 2026]

The spiraling clouds of a hurricane appear near the Hawaiian Islands. Its eye is just south of the Island of Hawaiʻi. [August 15, 2026]

Lala skirts south of the Island of Hawaiʻi as a category 1 hurricane in the right image, acquired by the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the Suomi NPP satellite on August 15, 2026, at about 1:45 p.m. Hawaii Standard Time (23:45 Universal Time). The storm decreased in intensity while tracking northwest and was a tropical storm when the VIIRS on the NOAA-20 satellite captured the left image about 24 hours later.

The Island of Hawaiʻi narrowly avoided a direct landfall by Hurricane Lala in mid-August 2026. The storm nonetheless delivered serious damage as it passed just south of the island on August 15 (above, right) as a category 1 storm on the Saffir-Simpson wind scale.

Lala brought rainfall totals exceeding 20 inches (50 centimeters) to parts of the island, causing flash flooding and ongoing mudflow risks. The highest rainfall total for the storm, 43.55 inches (110.6 centimeters) as of the morning of August 17, was recorded at Laupāhoehoe, on the coast northwest of Hilo. Lala downed trees, damaged bridges, and knocked homes off their foundations. Coastal areas were pummeled by large waves, while the summit of Mauna Kea, over 13,000 feet (4,000 meters) above sea level, experienced blizzard conditions.

By early afternoon on August 16, when the other image (left) was acquired, the storm had tracked northwest, roughly parallel to the island chain, and was southwest of Kauaʻi. Lala had decreased in intensity to a tropical storm, with sustained winds of 65 miles (105 kilometers) per hour, according to the National Hurricane Center.

While the Island of Hawaiʻi took the brunt of the storm, other islands also saw destructive effects. Strong winds caused widespread power outages, with more than 220,000 customers statewide without power as of the afternoon of August 16, according to news reports. Across the islands, wind and rain damaged infrastructure, and floodwaters and debris rendered roads impassable.

It has been an active tropical cyclone season in the Eastern Pacific so far in 2026, meteorologists note, consistent with what scientists expect during an El Niño, which has been underway as of mid-June. Warm water in the equatorial Pacific, the hallmark of El Niño, and the moisture and energy it transfers to the atmosphere help fuel nascent tropical storms. Lack of wind shear, another typical El Niño pattern in this region, also encourages tropical storms to develop and strengthen. The Atlantic hurricane season, in contrast, has been relatively calm, as greater wind shear over the Atlantic Ocean and Caribbean Sea during an El Niño inhibits hurricane formation by dissipating the upward motion of heat.

Sickinger hopes the crew will have the chance to make stops along the way to rest and recharge, but he is eager to reunite with his son.

"At some point, uh, we'll sit down together in some leather chairs and we'll have, you know, a cold drink of his choice, and he'll tell me all he can about his adventures," Sickinger said.

LAS VEGAS (AP) — The trial of Duane "Keffe D" Davis, the only person ever charged in the 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur, began Monday at the Clark County District Court Regional Justice Center in Las Vegas, 30 years after one of America's most high-profile unsolved killings.

Davis, 63, the former leader of the South Side Compton Crips, has pleaded not guilty to one count of murder with a deadly weapon and could face life in prison if convicted.

"Let's be clear, Duane Davis did not pull the trigger. But he did plan the shooting in retaliation for the beating of his nephew," Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal told jurors in his opening statement. "Remarkably, you will learn that from Duane Davis himself."

The case rests heavily on Davis's own statements over two decades: a confidential 1998 interview with the FBI, a 2008 interview with Los Angeles police detectives who were investigating the killing of rapper Biggie Smalls, a 2009 interview with Las Vegas police, and a 2019 memoir he co-authored, Compton Street Legend. In the 2008 interview, Davis said he passed a gun to the back seat of the car, and that his nephew Anderson fired.

Defense attorney Michael Sanft has attacked his own client's credibility, calling the years of statements and the memoir fiction. "They are telling you, they are representing as fact, when it's really fiction," Sanft told jurors.

On the second day of the trial, jurors were shown photos of Shakur's body and the casings recovered at the scene, and a forensic pathologist testified that a bullet entered Shakur's chest near his armpit and passed through his lung.

James "Mob James" McDonald, a former member of Shakur's entourage, took the stand. Knight, who is on the prosecution's witness list, has said he wants no part in the trial.

The prosecution is expected to call between 35 and 45 witnesses, and the trial is expected to last up to six weeks.

Chinese robot beats Usain Bolt's 100m world record at Beijing games

BEIJING (Reuters) — A Chinese humanoid robot ran 100 metres in 9.39 seconds in a preliminary heat at the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday, faster than the men's world record held by Jamaican sprinting great Usain Bolt.

Tiangong Ultra, developed by the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Center, won its heat at the opening of the second edition of the games, held at Beijing's National Speed Skating Oval, known as the Ice Ribbon. The robot overtook Honor's Lightning near the finish after falling behind early in the race; Lightning finished in 9.47 seconds, also faster than the 9.58-second record Bolt set at the 2009 World Athletics Championships.

At the end of the dash, the robots slammed into a cushion wall and fell to the ground to stop, and footage showed them being carried off on stretchers.

Before the opening, a humanoid robot from Chinese smartphone maker Honor completed a 100-metre sprint in 9.32 seconds during a trial of the games at a peak speed of 14.5 metres per second.

At last year's first edition of the games, the best time in the event was 21.50 seconds, so the new mark marks a leap in the running speed of humanoid robots.

More than 2,000 robots from 666 teams are competing in Beijing across 51 events. The games are being held the same week as the 2026 World Robot Conference, where thousands of products are on display.
</article>

<article>
US 50% tariffs on Canadian goods take effect; Carney vows retaliation

OTTAWA (Reuters) — Canada will impose tariffs on US goods in retaliation for the 50 percent levies that took effect just after midnight on Saturday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said, after three days of trade talks between the two neighbours collapsed.

The "dollar for dollar" tariffs on imports of US steel, dairy, household appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics will take effect on September 8, the Tuesday after Labor Day.

The new US tariffs cover roughly $20 billion of Canadian exports, about 5 percent of Canada's annual trade with the United States, and span sectors from wine to hockey equipment. They were ordered under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 and stack on top of a 10 percent levy imposed earlier this month.

President Donald Trump announced the 50 percent tariffs in an executive order on July 20, accusing Canada of "discriminatory treatment" in its trade policies. They were initially set to take effect on August 19 but Trump granted a three-day pause, saying the two countries were close to a deal.

The pause ran out without an agreement. Late on Friday, Carney said he was suspending trade negotiations and ordering Canadian negotiators back to Ottawa.

"We were not prepared to compromise Canada's sovereignty or undermine our key industries," Carney said in a 22-minute address to Canadians. "You're at war when you're attacked, and we got attacked."

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said there are no future talks planned with Canada and that Washington is moving forward with measures to respond to Canadian retaliation. The breakdown complicates the future of the USMCA free trade deal.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is hit hardest by the tariffs, said he backed Carney's position "tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar."

"We were not prepared to compromise Canada's sovereignty or undermine our key industries," Carney said in a 22-minute address to Canadians. "You're at war when you're attacked, and we got attacked."

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said there are no future talks planned with Canada and that Washington is moving forward with measures to respond to Canadian retaliation. The breakdown complicates the future of the USMCA free trade deal.

<article>
Evergrande founder Hui Ka Yan sentenced to life in prison

HONG KONG/SHENZHEN (Reuters) — The founder of China Evergrande Group, the world's most-indebted property developer, was sentenced to life in prison by a Chinese court on Thursday, five years after the firm's collapse shook the nation's economy and financial markets.

The Shenzhen Intermediate People's Court said it convicted 67-year-old Hui Ka Yan, also known as Xu Jiayin, of large-scale financial fraud in inflating the group's assets and concealing its liabilities, along with illegal fundraising and bribery. Hui, once Forbes Asia's richest man, pleaded guilty in April to eight charges.

The court ordered the confiscation of all of Hui's personal property, with political rights revoked for life, and said restitution for victims takes priority over state fines and asset seizures.

Evergrande Group was fined 8.82 billion yuan ($1.31 billion) and Evergrande Real Estate Group, its major mainland subsidiary, was fined 7 billion yuan ($1.04 billion), a combined 15.82 billion yuan (about $2.35 billion).

Five other senior executives were sentenced to prison terms ranging from six to 18 years, and 56 people in total were sentenced in connection with the collapse, state media reported.

Hui was separately fined 47 million yuan and banned from China's securities markets for life by the China Securities Regulatory Commission in 2024 over inflating company financial results.

At its peak, Evergrande employed about 200,000 people, and its default in 2021 triggered a property crisis that spread across the industry.
</article>

The Shenzhen Intermediate People's Court said it convicted 67-year-old Hui Ka Yan, also known as Xu Jiayin, of large-scale financial fraud in inflating the group's assets and concealing its liabilities, along with illegal fundraising and bribery. Hui, once Forbes Asia's richest man, pleaded guilty in April to eight charges.

The court ordered the confiscation of all of Hui's personal property, with political rights revoked for life, and said restitution for victims takes priority over state fines and asset seizures.

Evergrande Group was fined 8.82 billion yuan ($1.31 billion) and Evergrande Real Estate Group, its major mainland subsidiary, was fined 7 billion yuan ($1.04 billion), a combined 15.82 billion yuan (about $2.35 billion).

Five other senior executives were sentenced to prison terms ranging from six to 18 years, and 56 people in total were sentenced in connection with the collapse, state media reported.

Hui was separately fined 47 million yuan and banned from China's securities markets for life by the China Securities Regulatory Commission in 2024 over inflating company financial results.

At its peak, Evergrande employed about 200,000 people, and its default in 2021 triggered a property crisis that spread across the industry.
</article>

PORT-AU-PRINCE (AP) — At least 47 people were killed and more than 50 others kidnapped after armed men attacked a once-peaceful community near Haiti's capital earlier this week, the United Nations said Tuesday.

The mayor said two government employees were among the killed, including his cousin, who served as his security detail.

The mayor said members of Viv Ansanm, the gang coalition that the United States has designated as a foreign terrorist organization, also set fire to 25 homes.

Gang violence has displaced a record 1.5 million people across Haiti, where more than 3,050 people were reported killed from January to June, the U.N. said.

Those released had been granted "alternative measures from incarceration" under the Program for Peace and Democratic Coexistence, the country's interim government said on Friday, in a statement distributed by communications minister Miguel Perez Pirela. The releases took place at El Rodeo I prison in Guatire, in the Miranda state.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the release of more than 130 political prisoners was "a crucial step for the nation's reconciliation process." Since the US overthrew and detained Maduro on January 3, 1,046 Venezuelans have been released, Rubio added.

The move comes after the first round of US-brokered reconciliation talks between the government and the opposition, which kicked off last week and wrapped up on Wednesday. The talks are being led by opposition figure Dinorah Figuera and National Assembly President Jorge Rodriguez, the brother of interim President Delcy Rodriguez, who took over as Maduro's deputy.

The opposition movement Vente Venezuela said it had independently verified the release of 43 detainees as of 4:58 p.m. local time and that it was continuing to review individual cases. The Foro Penal rights group confirmed the release of at least 40 political prisoners.

As of Monday, Foro Penal said 391 political prisoners remained behind bars.

Opposition figure Juan Pablo Guanipa welcomed the releases but demanded that all political prisoners be freed "without exception, without delay, and promptly," saying each person returning home is "an immense relief" for families who have "suffered too much."
</article>

<article>
Renaissance paintings by Antonello da Messina stolen from Sicilian museum

MESSINA (AP) — Four of the most important works of art by the 15th-century Renaissance master Antonello da Messina were stolen during a national holiday from a museum in the Sicilian port city of Messina.

Thieves gained access to the Regional Interdisciplinary Museum, or MuMe, at around 9:50 p.m. on Saturday as the city celebrated Ferragosto and the La Vara religious festival. Three or four masked intruders entered through a side gate where part of the perimeter railing was bent or cut, forced an exterior door, and reached the rooms where the works were kept. The museum's alarms and video surveillance systems were functioning, and the robbery took just a few minutes.

All five surviving wooden panels of the San Gregorio Polyptych, an altarpiece signed and dated to 1473, were removed from their frames, but the thieves abandoned two of them against a low wall outside the museum, where a citizen noticed them and called police. The third stolen work was a small double-sided panel taken from an armored display case, depicting the Virgin and Child with a Franciscan monk on one side and the dead Christ on the other.

<article>
Panama Canal to limit ship transits due to El Niño drought

PANAMA CITY (DW) — The Panama Canal will cut the number of ships passing through it starting next month because of drought caused by the El Niño phenomenon, the operator of the strategic waterway linking the Atlantic and Pacific said on Thursday.

The Panama Canal Authority (ACP) announced temporary modifications to the locks' transit capacity, including adjustments to its daily auctions, walking back a previous pledge not to limit vessel passage. Under the new measures, the canal will limit daily transits to 34 vessels, down from the current cap of 36, as of September 3. From September 15, the number of ships permitted will drop to 32.

The cuts are driven by low water levels in the two artificial lakes, Gatun and Alajuela, that feed the canal. Rainfall between May and August was about 34% below the historical average for the period, the canal operator said, and water contributions to the basin were 44% below the historical average.

Central America is in the throes of a severe drought driven by El Niño, a weather pattern that warms surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean. Scientists expect the 2026-2027 El Niño to be particularly strong, possibly among the strongest on record, and Panama Canal administrator Ricaurte Vasquez warned it could last much longer than usual.

The 50-mile (80-kilometer) canal carries around 5% of global maritime trade. Through June 2026 it averaged 35 daily transits, against a capacity of roughly 40 per day.

The waterway was also hit by severe drought in 2023-2024. In 2023, lake water levels were so low that the operator cut daily ship transits from 38 to 22.

The ACP also postponed further draft restrictions: the maximum authorized draft of 14.63 meters in the Neopanamax locks was delayed to September 2, and the reduction to 14.48 meters to October 1.

Indonesia: Dozens dead after earthquake off Flores island
Shakeel Sobhan, Karl Sexton, with AFP, AP, Reuters | DW, August 15, 2026

At least 47 people have died and several buildings were damaged after the powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake, which was followed by dozens of aftershocks. A tsunami warning has been lifted.

A powerful earthquake struck off the coast of Indonesia early on Saturday, killing at least 47 people and toppling buildings, the National Disaster Mitigation Agency said.

The epicenter of the magnitude 7.7 earthquake hit off the coast of the island of Flores at a shallow depth of 10 kilometers (6.2 miles), the US Geological Survey (USGS) said.

Shallow earthquakes (up to 70 kilometers deep) are considered more dangerous and destructive.

Tsunami waves of less than 1 meter (3 feet) were recorded in several areas of the country before the warning was lifted about three hours after the quake.

Where did the earthquake strike?

Indonesia's Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics Agency (BMKG) recorded the first quake at 4:58 am (2158 GMT) at a depth of 15 km (9 miles), followed by dozens of aftershocks.

People rushed out onto the street as the quake struck.

Video shared on social media from Maumere, the main town in Sikka Regency on Flores Island in eastern Indonesia, showed part of a building collapsing in a cloud of dust and rubble as people screamed and ran into the street.

"Many buildings here were damaged ... I saw that the waiting room at the Pelni port terminal in Maumere had collapsed," Yohanna Embu, a resident of Sikka, a regency within East Nusa Tenggara province, told AP.

Residents evacuated, tsunami warning lifted

The initial jolt was followed by a series of aftershocks in the same area, including one of magnitude 6.1.

BMKG issued a tsunami warning for part of East Nusa Tenggara, West Nusa Tenggara, South Sulawesi and Southeast Sulawesi provinces, urging residents to stay away from beaches and riverbanks.

The tsunami warning was later lifted.

"We have ended (the tsunami warning) but we will keep monitoring the sea level," Wijayanto, earthquake and tsunami director at BMKG, said.

Before the tsunami warning was lifted, residents of Maumere on Flores Island were told to move to higher ground, according to AFP.

State television also showed hundreds of people evacuating in nearby Nagekeo regency.

Local TV footage showed a hospital in the district of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara Province moving patients outside.

Authorities assessing damage, casualties

The quake caused severe damage and collapsed buildings, causing power outages in cities and villages, severely hindering rescue operations.

"We are continuing to collect reports of damages and casualties, but there are communication disruptions," East Nusa Tenggara police chief Rudi Darmoko said.

Local television reports showed patients at several hospitals being evacuated from buildings as a precaution.

"Our students and nuns ran out in panic beneath a collapsing roof," Guidelbertus Tanga, rector of Ritapiret Seminary on Flores said. "At least one priest suffered a broken leg after jumping from the second floor of a building during the quake."

There were also damages reported in some part of southern Sulawesi island.

Why does Indonesia keep getting hit by major earthquakes?

Indonesia is located on the so-called "Ring of Fire," a region of heightened seismic activity in the Pacific basin that stretches from Southeast Asia to Japan.

Here are some of the biggest earthquakes to strike the region:

1992, magnitude 7: A tsunami following a strong earthquake on the southeastern island of Flores killed about 2,500 people.

2004, magnitude 9.1: A quake struck off the coast of Sumatra triggering a tsunami that killed 170,000 in Indonesia and 220,000 in several countries in the Indian Ocean.

2018, magnitude 6.9: A tremor killed more than 550 people on the islands of Lombok and Sumbawa.

2018, magnitude 7.5: A quake and a subsequent tsunami in Palu on Sulawesi island left more than 4,300 people dead or missing.

"Please heed all warnings from local officials, evacuate immediately if you are ordered to do so, and do not put yourself or first responders at risk."

The declaration directs all state agencies to work through the Nevada Emergency Operations Center, and the governor authorized one CH-47 Chinook helicopter, one UH-60 Black Hawk and 72 National Guard security personnel to support the response.

<article>
US national debt tops $40 trillion for the first time

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — Total US debt has topped $40 trillion for the first time, the Treasury Department said on Wednesday, drawing fresh warnings that a fiscal crisis is brewing as ballooning costs for social safety-net programs and interest payments far outstrip revenues held back by tax cuts.

The Treasury's latest daily cash and debt balances statement showed total public debt outstanding at $40.047 trillion on Tuesday, a total that includes Treasury securities held by the public of $32.266 trillion and intra-governmental debt holdings of $7.782 trillion.

The milestone has arrived faster than forecasters expected. A decade ago, the national debt stood at about $19.4 trillion, so the government's total borrowing has more than doubled in ten years.

The Congressional Joint Economic Committee calculated that the debt is now growing at roughly $90,000 every second. At a population of about 343 million, the $40 trillion total works out to approximately $117,000 per person.

Treasury also reported a $432.3 billion deficit for July, the highest monthly total in more than five years, with the year-to-date shortfall nearing $1.8 trillion.

The Washington Post reported that the landmark figure was reached months earlier than some models predicted, in part because of billions of dollars in lost revenue from President Donald Trump's invalidated tariffs.

The public share of the debt is now near 100 percent of GDP, and the total passed $30 trillion just four and a half years ago.
</article>

The Treasury's latest daily cash and debt balances statement showed total public debt outstanding at $40.047 trillion on Tuesday, a total that includes Treasury securities held by the public of $32.266 trillion and intra-governmental debt holdings of $7.782 trillion.

The milestone has arrived faster than forecasters expected. A decade ago, the national debt stood at about $19.4 trillion, so the government's total borrowing has more than doubled in ten years.

The Congressional Joint Economic Committee calculated that the debt is now growing at roughly $90,000 every second. At a population of about 343 million, the $40 trillion total works out to approximately $117,000 per person.

Treasury also reported a $432.3 billion deficit for July, the highest monthly total in more than five years, with the year-to-date shortfall nearing $1.8 trillion.

The Washington Post reported that the landmark figure was reached months earlier than some models predicted, in part because of billions of dollars in lost revenue from President Donald Trump's invalidated tariffs.

The public share of the debt is now near 100 percent of GDP, and the total passed $30 trillion just four and a half years ago.
</article>

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — Total US debt has topped $40 trillion for the first time, the Treasury Department said on Wednesday, drawing fresh warnings that a fiscal crisis is brewing as ballooning costs for social safety-net programs and interest payments far outstrip revenues held back by tax cuts.

The Treasury's latest daily cash and debt balances statement showed total public debt outstanding at $40.047 trillion on Tuesday, a total that includes Treasury securities held by the public of $32.266 trillion and intra-governmental debt holdings of $7.782 trillion.

The milestone has arrived faster than forecasters expected. A decade ago, the national debt stood at about $19.4 trillion, so the government's total borrowing has more than doubled in ten years.

The Congressional Joint Economic Committee calculated that the debt is now growing at roughly $90,000 every second. At a population of about 343 million, the $40 trillion total works out to approximately $117,000 per person.

Treasury also reported a $432.3 billion deficit for July, the highest monthly total in more than five years, with the year-to-date shortfall nearing $1.8 trillion.

The Washington Post reported that the landmark figure was reached months earlier than some models predicted, in part because of billions of dollars in lost revenue from President Donald Trump's invalidated tariffs.

The public share of the debt is now near 100 percent of GDP, and the total passed $30 trillion just four and a half years ago.
</article>

WASHINGTON (Reuters) — Total US debt has topped $40 trillion for the first time, the Treasury Department said on Wednesday, drawing fresh warnings that a fiscal crisis is brewing as ballooning costs for social safety-net programs and interest payments far outstrip revenues held back by tax cuts.

The Treasury's latest daily cash and debt balances statement showed total public debt outstanding at $40.047 trillion on Tuesday, a total that includes Treasury securities held by the public of $32.266 trillion and intra-governmental debt holdings of $7.782 trillion.

The milestone has arrived faster than forecasters expected. A decade ago, the national debt stood at about $19.4 trillion, so the government's total borrowing has more than doubled in ten years.

The Congressional Joint Economic Committee calculated that the debt is now growing at roughly $90,000 every second. At a population of about 343 million, the $40 trillion total works out to approximately $117,000 per person.

Treasury also reported a $432.3 billion deficit for July, the highest monthly total in more than five years, with the year-to-date shortfall nearing $1.8 trillion.

The Washington Post reported that the landmark figure was reached months earlier than some models predicted, in part because of billions of dollars in lost revenue from President Donald Trump's invalidated tariffs.

The public share of the debt is now near 100 percent of GDP, and the total passed $30 trillion just four and a half years ago.

US launches 'Operation Economic Outcast' against Iran

WASHINGTON (AP) — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday announced a new campaign of financial sanctions against Iran, warning every country that does business with the Islamic Republic to sever those ties or face retaliation from the United States.

Bessent dubbed the campaign "Operation Economic Outcast" and an "economic D-Day," likening it to the Allied landings in France in the Second World War. "Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," he said.

The announcement followed President Donald Trump's pledge last week to unleash an "economic D-Day" against Tehran and his declaration that countries doing business with Iran would face "tremendous economic consequences."

The Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned nearly 60 entities, individuals and vessels in multiple jurisdictions, including in the United Arab Emirates, Hong Kong, China, Singapore and Switzerland, accusing them of enabling the Iranian regime's oil, nuclear, missile and cyber networks. Treasury said the new sanctions target five sectors: cryptocurrency used by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and regime insiders, weapons-related technologies, gold, Iran's airlines and shipping.

Bessent said the United States had been engaged in "quiet diplomacy" with Iran's trade partners, warning that any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system. "No one is above the reach of US sanctions," he said.

China, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates are Iran's largest trade partners. Ahead of Monday's announcement, the United Arab Emirates said it was ending all trade relations with Iran.

HARARE (AP) — The death toll from an overloaded ferry that capsized on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe last week rose to 80 after eight more bodies were recovered on Sunday, police said.

The town of Kariba sits nearly 280 kilometres northwest of the capital, Harare, and the ferry was a vital link for the rural communities living around the lake, which shares its waters with Zambia.

Survivors said they had pleaded with the driver to turn back as the water turned rough.

The government-run passenger ferry, the Mbuya Nehanda, overturned in choppy water on Tuesday while travelling from the town of Kariba toward rural and fishing communities in the country's northwest, where roads are damaged and public transport is scarce. The disaster is believed to be the deadliest of its kind in the country's history.

Officials say the boat was authorised to carry 90 people, but reports indicate it was carrying 114 adults and five crew members, together with an unspecified number of children. Zimbabwe's disaster management agency said 77 people were rescued.

Search teams recovered 25 bodies on Saturday, taking the toll to 72, before Sunday's further recoveries. Police said the search is continuing, guided by information from relatives, and that the exact passenger manifest has not been established.

Among the dead are children, according to authorities, and hundreds of people gathered at the district hospital in Kariba to identify the bodies of their relatives. The town of Kariba sits nearly 280 kilometres northwest of the capital, Harare, and the ferry was a vital link for the rural communities living around the lake, which shares its waters with Zambia.

Survivors said they had pleaded with the driver to turn back as the water turned rough.
</article>

Bangladesh elects its president in first contested vote in 35 years

DHAKA (AP) — Bangladesh's parliament on Thursday elected ruling party veteran Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir as the country's 23rd president in the first contested presidential election in 35 years.

Central African Republic closes gold mine that killed more than 100

BANGUI (AP) — The Central African Republic's government on Saturday shut down a gold mining site that killed more than 100 people when it collapsed earlier this week, citing non-compliance with regulatory procedures.

Ruffin Benam Beltoungou, the minister of mines and geology, announced the closure of the Zamboye site in the western part of the country, citing "non-compliance with mining standards and non-compliance with administrative directives," as an investigation continues.

The artisanal mine caved in Tuesday in the village of Zamboye, near the border with Cameroon. Ruffin Benam Beltoungou, the minister of mines and geology, announced the closure of the Zamboye site in the western part of the country, citing "non-compliance with mining standards and non-compliance with administrative directives," as an investigation continues.

The artisanal mine caved in Tuesday in the village of Zamboye, near the border with Cameroon. Local officials and the Red Cross said Wednesday that more than 100 people had died in the collapse and warned the toll was likely to rise, while the mines ministry put the official toll at 49, a breakdown of 34 Central Africans, 13 Cameroonians and two Chadians.

The minister visited the site on Wednesday. Seven injured people were taken to a hospital in Baboua, about 50 kilometres from the mining site, and rescue operations were at times suspended because the mine continued to collapse and heavy rains had flooded lower sections of the pit.

The site, locally known as Moscow-RCA, is a sprawling open-pit mine beside the Kadei River, which forms part of the border with Cameroon, and thousands of people in the area depend on it. The Zamboye site had been closed before the accident, but illegal miners still worked there.

The Baboua prosecutor's office opened a judicial investigation to establish the cause of the collapse and who was running the site. Search for survivors by local workers was hampered by a lack of expertise and equipment for the scale of the disaster.
</article>

Merck, Moderna say personalized mRNA vaccine met goals in late-stage melanoma trial

RAHWAY, N.J. (Reuters) — Moderna and Merck said on Wednesday that a personalized mRNA cancer vaccine reduced the risk of melanoma returning or spreading in a late-stage trial, a milestone in a new field of cancer treatment that sent Moderna's shares surging as much as 160%.

The companies announced positive topline results from the Phase 3 INTerpath-001 trial evaluating intismeran autogene, an mRNA-based individualized neoantigen therapy, in combination with Merck's immunotherapy Keytruda (pembrolizumab), compared with Keytruda alone.

At a pre-specified interim analysis, the combination demonstrated statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements in the primary endpoint of recurrence-free survival (RFS) and the key secondary endpoint of distant metastasis-free survival (DMFS) in patients with completely resected stage IIB-IV cutaneous melanoma who had not received prior systemic therapy.

The trial enrolled 1,137 patients, randomized 2:1 to receive intismeran, dosed every three weeks for up to nine doses, with Keytruda every six weeks for up to nine cycles, versus Keytruda alone for approximately one year. The study will continue to evaluate other key endpoints, including overall survival.

This is the first positive Phase 3 readout for an individualized neoantigen therapy and for an mRNA-based cancer therapy, the companies said. The data will be presented at an upcoming international medical meeting, and the partners plan to engage with regulators on filing submissions.

Moderna President Stephen Hoge said thousands of patients who have undergone surgery to remove high-risk melanoma tumors could benefit as soon as next year if regulators approve the vaccine.

The Phase 3 results build on five-year follow-up data from the Phase 2b KEYNOTE-942 trial, presented at the 2026 ASCO Annual Meeting, in which the combination reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 49% and the risk of distant metastasis or death by 59% compared with Keytruda alone.

Merck and Moderna have been research partners since 2016. Merck paid $200 million upfront to begin the alliance and $250 million in 2022 to exercise its option for intismeran.

Ebola outbreak in DR Congo becomes deadliest in its history

KINSHASA (AFP) — The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has killed 2,325 people, surpassing the death toll of the 2018-2020 outbreak to become the deadliest in the country's history, public health officials said on Sunday.

DR Congo's Institute of Public Health said it had recorded 4,945 confirmed cases, including 101 in the previous 24 hours. The latest government data shows that the total number of deaths has surpassed the 2,299 deaths recorded in the 2018-2020 outbreak, which was previously the country's worst on record.

The outbreak, declared by national authorities on 15 May, is the 17th to have emerged in DR Congo since Ebola was discovered 50 years ago. It became the country's largest in terms of total confirmed cases in late July, and researchers say it may have been spreading undetected since February.

It is the fastest-growing outbreak in the known history of the virus: the world's deadliest, in West Africa in 2014-2016, took close to five months to reach 1,000 fatalities, while the current outbreak reached 2,000 deaths in under three months. The World Health Organization has said the outbreak is on track to surpass the 2014-2016 outbreak, which killed 11,325 people across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.

The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain. As of 19 August, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reported 5,290 confirmed cases and 2,516 deaths, with 837 people hospitalised in Ituri, North Kivu and Haut-Uele provinces. The virus has spread to Uganda, and Europe has recorded its first imported case.

Infections among health workers continue, with at least 155 confirmed cases, including 45 deaths.

On Thursday, the UN's International Coordinating Group, led by the WHO, allocated 70,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine, developed by Merck, to DR Congo. Ervebo is approved for the Zaire strain, used in the 2018 and 2020 DRC outbreaks, and has not been evaluated against Bundibugyo, the strain in this outbreak, so the doses will be used in a Phase 3 trial of the Zaire vaccine against Bundibugyo. The ICG had already allocated 56,000 Ervebo doses for DRC outbreaks between 2021 and July 2026.
